newsitem.title: USA: Senate panel okays bill for veterans, housing.
newsitem.headline: Senate panel okays bill for veterans, housing.

text.p: The Senate Appropriations Committee Thursday approved a $91 billion spending bill for next year's programmes for veterans, housing, environmental protection, space and science.

The bill is $1.4 billion below the Clinton administration's request, with some funds shifted from the Environmental Protection Agency to pull up spending for veterans. Veterans programmes make up nearly half of the bill's spending.
But unlike last year, this bill was free of "environmental riders" or measures to restrict the EPA from enforcing a variety of regulations.
The House passed its version of the $91 billion spending bill Wednesday, which also was free of contentious riders.

"Protecting VA medical care means that fulfilling the president's full request for EPA -- for which a 12 percent or $850 million increase was requested -- simply was not possible," Missouri Republican Christopher Bond, who chaired the key subcommittee, said.
The bill boosts spending for veterans $92 million above the administration's request in programmes for medical care, research and housing.

Barbara Mikulski of Maryland, ranking subcommittee Democrat, said she was working with the administration to find offsetting spending cuts to put some of the president's priorities back in the bill when it reaches the Senate floor.
The bill would fund the EPA at $7 billion, up $180 million from this year but $680 million below the White House request.

The committee balked at the White House call for a 50 percent increase in the Superfund hazardous waste programme, as Republicans said the troubled programme should be reformed first. However Congress and the administration have been at loggerheads for several years on how to fix the programme.
The bill also would restore $275 million to a revolving fund to help states undertake projects to ensure safe drinking water supplies.
The bill funds the Department of Housing and Urban Development at $25.4 billion, and restores $635 million in funding for the elderly and disabled that were cut in the White House plan.

It also funds the National Aeronautic and Space Administration at $13.5 billion, matching the White House request; the National Science Foundation at $3.4 billion, $10 million above the request; and the Federal Emergency Management Agency at at $788 million, matching the request.
In a move to please President Clinton, the bill keeps the AmeriCorps volunteer community service programme at $400.5 million.

The House version cut that programme in half, but House Appropriations Committee leaders said they expected the Senate to restore full funding for one of Clinton's prized programmes to get his signature on the final bill from Congress.
